characters: STRICT RULE FOR EVERY FILM: no Sikh Guru appears in any picture in any form (no face, no back, no silhouette, no hands, no shadow, no figure on a throne or platform, no glowing outline). Where a Guru is in the story, show only the sangat (the people), places, objects and light, with the Guru's position out of frame. Recurring historical people: THE BHATT POETS (film 1): three court poets, men 40-60, long dark beards streaked grey, cream and rust-red robes, rolled palm-leaf and paper manuscripts tied with red thread. EMPEROR AKBAR (film 2): man about 40, trimmed dark moustache, no full beard, pale gold silk jama, jewelled white turban with a plume, pearl necklaces; his guards in green and maroon. DAYA RAM (film 4): shopkeeper from Lahore, about 30, lean, dark beard, plain white kurta and simple off-white turban; with him THE FOUR WHO FOLLOW: a sturdy farmer (35, sun-dark, brown cloth), a water-carrier (25, wiry, goatskin water bag), a cloth printer (40, blue-and-red dyed fingers), a barber (30, small cloth roll of tools at his waist); after the tent all five wear matching saffron robes with blue sashes and saffron turbans, swords held upright. BHAI GHANAIYA (film 5): man about 50, kind lined face, white beard, plain white clothes and white turban, a brown goatskin water bag (mashk) on his shoulder. BABA BUDDHA (film 7): very old man, long snow-white beard, white robes and turban, gentle. Mughal-era soldiers wear green, maroon and steel; early Sikhs wear saffron, blue and white. THE MODERN FAMILY (last picture of every film, Bay Area or Southall-style suburb, today): SIMRAN, 17, long black braid, often a light chunni over her hair, oversized hoodie or denim jacket, steel kara on her right wrist, small gold nose stud; JAS, her brother, 14, navy blue patka, black puffer jacket, sneakers, steel kara; THEIR DAD, mid-40s, full beard flecked with grey, crisp saffron or navy dastar, plaid flannel shirt; THEIR MOM, mid-40s, shoulder-length hair under a pale pink chunni, cardigan; BIJI, their grandmother, 70s, white chunni, round glasses, cream salwar kameez. Warm, cool, everyday, never posed or corny.

1.story: The Bhatt court poets and the cry 'wahe guru', their swayyas in the Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1389-1409 (Waheguru at Ang 1402-1404)
1.point: Waheguru, the Sikh name for God, means 'wow, the teacher': not a title but a cry of wonder, because Sikh scripture says God is beyond describing.
1.script: A family of court poets came to the Sikh Gurus. The Bhatts. Their whole job was praising kings, in the biggest words money could buy. Now they wanted to praise the Gurus, and the God they pointed to. So they tried. Bigger words. Grander lines. Nothing was big enough. Sikh scripture says God is beyond counting, beyond describing. So their poems, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, break into one cry: wahe guru. Wow. The teacher. That's the name Sikhs say for God. Not a title, like king. A reaction. When words run out, you say wow. Good news? Waheguru. Hard news? Waheguru. It points past the feeling, to what's bigger.

open.text: the best poets ran out of *words.*

pictures: Picture 1: Late 1500s Punjab, golden afternoon. The three Bhatt poets walk a dusty road toward a small town by a shining pool, manuscripts under their arms, robes catching the wind. Wide shot, poets small against big sky and green fields. No Guru anywhere.

Picture 2: Flashback to a rich king's marble court. The poets stand reciting before a jewelled king on a high throne, courtiers in silk, gold everywhere; the poets' faces are proud and practised. Warm lamp light, ornate pillars.

Picture 3: Night, a simple room. One poet sits on the floor by a single oil lamp, surrounded by crumpled and crossed-out pages, pen raised, stuck, eyes wide. The other two lean in, frowning. Close, intimate, lamp glow on faces.

Picture 4: The poet steps outside into an enormous starry sky over the fields; stars beyond counting, the Milky Way pouring overhead, the man tiny at the bottom of the frame, head tilted back. Deep blue and silver.

Picture 5: Dawn in a gathering of ordinary Sikhs (the sangat) seated on the floor under a plain canopy. The poet stands among them, arms opened wide, mouth open in a joyful cry, morning light pouring in from the side. Camera behind the seated people; the front of the space is out of frame, only soft light. No Guru figure.

Picture 6: TODAY. A kitchen in a modern suburban home. Simran, 17, holds up her phone, jumping with good news (a college acceptance on screen, no readable text); Jas, 14, in his navy patka, cheers; Biji in her white chunni, hands pressed together, eyes closed in a happy smile, clearly saying the word. Warm evening light, everyday clutter, real and cool.

Gentle pan up from the reciting poets to the glittering king as lamp flames flicker.
Slow push in on the stuck poet's face while the lamp flame trembles and a crumpled page settles.
Slow tilt up from the small man into the vast turning star field.
Light grows across the seated crowd as the poet's arms open; slight handheld drift toward him.

2.story: Emperor Akbar sits in the pangat before meeting Guru Amar Das at Goindwal ('pehle pangat, phir sangat'), Sikh tradition
2.point: Langar is the free Sikh community kitchen where everyone, even an emperor, sits on the floor in one row and eats the same food, so nobody sits higher.
2.script: The emperor of India, Akbar, rode to the small town of Goindwal to meet the third Sikh Guru. Silk, jewels, guards. But at the door, he was told the rule. First the meal, then the meeting. Sit in the row. So the most powerful man in India took off his shoes, sat down on the floor between farmers and laborers, and ate the same simple food from the same kitchen. That kitchen is the langar. Free. Vegetarian. Open to anyone, of any faith or none. No chairs, so nobody sits higher. At school, where you sit says who you are. In the langar row, it can't.

open.text: the emperor of india sat on the *floor.*

pictures: Picture 1: Punjab, 1500s. Emperor Akbar's procession approaches the small riverside town of Goindwal: elephants and horses, banners, guards in green and maroon, the emperor on horseback in gold silk and jewelled turban. Wide, dusty golden light, the plain town ahead.

Picture 2: The plain doorway of the langar. A humble Sikh volunteer in simple white clothes, hands joined politely, gestures toward the rows of people eating on the floor inside. Akbar pauses, eyebrows raised; his guards bristle behind him. Mid shot. No Guru anywhere.

Picture 3: Inside, Akbar sits cross-legged on a long woven floor mat, shoes left at the door, between a sun-dark farmer and a dusty laborer, all in one long row. The farmer glances sideways at him in disbelief. Warm side light through the doorway.

Picture 4: Close on hands: a volunteer's hands lay a warm roti into Akbar's ringed, cupped palms, and the very same roti into the rough hands of the laborer beside him. Steam, simple brass plates of dal.
Picture 5: The kitchen: huge iron pots over wood fires, volunteers of every age stirring dal and rolling rotis, steam rising into beams of sunlight. Busy, joyful, wide.

Picture 6: TODAY. A big modern gurdwara langar hall. Jas, 14, in his navy patka, serves dal from a steel bucket down a long row; Simran hands out rotis; sitting on the floor in the row are a business guy in a suit, a delivery rider, an elderly white couple, students with backpacks, all heads covered with bandanas or scarves. Bright, real, everyday.
motion: Slow tracking shot alongside the procession as banners ripple and dust lifts.
Gentle push in on Akbar's surprised face while the volunteer's hand stays open toward the rows.
Slow lateral slide along the row, ending on Akbar between the farmer and laborer.
Hands move in: the roti is placed into each pair of palms as steam curls up.
Camera drifts through the steam past stirring ladles and turning rotis.
Tracking shot down the row as Jas ladles dal and people smile up at him.

3.story: Guru Gobind Singh makes the turban (dastar) over uncut hair (kesh) part of every Sikh's identity, when fine turbans marked kings and nobles; Sikh tradition and Sikh Rehat Maryada
3.point: The Sikh turban isn't a hat: it's a crown tied fresh each day over uncut hair, given to every Sikh whatever family they came from.
3.script: In the world of the Gurus, a fine turban meant one thing. Power. Kings wore them. Nobles wore them. A farmer? A barber? Not them. Then the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, asked his Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, as it grew, and made the turban part of who they are. Whatever family they came from. So the farmer tied one. So did the barber. Suddenly, ordinary people walked through the market wearing crowns. That's the dastar. Not a hat that comes off with the weather. A crown, tied fresh each morning, over hair left as it grew. The first try always comes out lopsided. Every try is still a crown you tie yourself.
beats: In the world of the Gurus
pictures: Picture 1: A 1600s Mughal-era street. A noble rides through on a white horse, wearing a towering jewelled turban with a feather plume and pearls, attendants with a parasol. Crowds part. Rich, gold-and-crimson palette, low angle making him loom.

Picture 2: In the crowd, a sun-dark farmer and a barber (tool roll at his waist) in plain rough cloth watch the noble pass, eyes lowered. Mid shot, dusty light, the noble's plume blurred in the foreground.

Picture 3: A green hillside at Anandpur. A large crowd of ordinary Sikhs sits listening, seen from behind, faces turned toward the front, where there is only a tall saffron flag on a pole and bright morning light; the front of the gathering is out of frame. No Guru figure of any kind.

Picture 4: Dawn by a village well. The farmer, hair long and combed into a knot, wraps a long length of saffron cloth around his head, layer by layer, concentrating; beside him the barber ties a deep blue one. Soft pink sky, close and warm.

Picture 5: A busy market. The farmer, the barber, a water-carrier and a potter stride through in crisp saffron, blue and white turbans, chins up, sunlight on them; a noble at a stall looks twice. Wide, proud, vivid.

Picture 6: TODAY. A bathroom mirror in the morning. Jas, 14, attempts his first full dastar, navy cloth comically lopsided; his dad behind him, in a crisp saffron dastar, laughs and fixes one fold; Simran leans in the doorway with her phone, grinning. Warm morning light, toothpaste on the counter, real and cool.

Rack focus from the blurred plume to the farmer's lowered eyes.
Slow drift over the backs of the seated crowd as the saffron flag ripples in the breeze.
Close slow orbit as the cloth wraps around once more and settles.
Tracking shot walking alongside the men as cloth tails flutter and the noble turns his head.
Gentle push in on the mirror as the dad tucks the fold and Jas cracks up.

4.story: Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur: the call for a head, the tent, and the Panj Pyare; Sikh tradition
4.point: The Panj Pyare, 'five beloved', were five strangers from different castes and corners of India who stood up and walked out as one family, the first of the Khalsa.
4.script: Spring, 1699. A huge crowd on a hillside at Anandpur, for the harvest festival. Then the tenth Guru steps out with a drawn sword and asks: who will give their head for the faith? Silence. One man stands. Daya Ram, a shopkeeper. He follows the Guru into a tent. The Guru comes out alone, and asks again. Four more stand, one at a time. A farmer. A water-carrier. A cloth printer. A barber. What happened in that tent, the tellings differ. But all five walked out alive, dressed alike, side by side. Five castes that would never share a meal. One family: the Panj Pyare, the five beloved. Family isn't only blood. It's who stands up beside you.

open.text: five went into the tent. *five* came out.

4.drop: But all five walked out alive
beats: But all five walked out alive
pictures: Picture 1: Spring 1699, the green hills of Anandpur. A huge festival crowd covers the hillside, saffron and blue banners, wheat fields gold below, morning sun. Epic wide shot.

Picture 2: The crowd's faces, seen from the front, gone suddenly still and afraid, all looking up toward a platform that is out of frame above the camera. A single hard line of sunlight, like the flash off a blade, cuts across their faces. No Guru, no figure on the platform, only the people's reaction.
Picture 3: In the seated, frozen crowd, one man rises alone: Daya Ram, lean, white kurta, off-white turban, face calm and pale. Heads turn toward him. Mid shot, the crowd soft around him.

Picture 4: A plain cloth tent at the edge of the gathering, its flap closed, shifting in the wind. The crowd watches it from a distance, holding their breath. Only the tent and the people; nobody at the entrance. Long shadows.

Picture 5: Across the crowd, four more men stand up one after another: the sturdy farmer, the wiry water-carrier with his goatskin bag, the cloth printer with blue-and-red dyed fingers, the barber with his tool roll. Wide, each lit by a shaft of sun.

Picture 6: The tent flap open: the five step out alive, side by side, in matching saffron robes with blue sashes and saffron turbans, swords held upright, faces bright and steady. The crowd gasps and rises. No Guru in the frame or the doorway behind them.

Picture 7: TODAY. A Vaisakhi parade on a suburban street, cherry trees in bloom. Five Sikhs in saffron lead the procession, swords upright. On the curb, Simran, 17, in a denim jacket and chunni, links arms with two friends of different backgrounds; Jas waves a small saffron flag from a low wall beside Dad; Biji claps. Bright, crowded, joyful.
motion: Slow aerial drift over the hillside crowd as banners ripple.
The line of light slides across the frozen faces; very slow push in.
Slow push in on Daya Ram as he rises and heads turn.
Locked-off shot; only the tent flap and the crowd's clothes stir in the wind.
Camera pans across the crowd as each of the four rises in turn.
Slow push back as the five walk forward and the crowd rises around them.
Tracking shot down the curb past Simran and her friends as the five pass.

5.story: Bhai Ghanaiya gives water to the wounded of both sides at Anandpur (Sikh tradition), and the Ardas' closing words 'sarbat da bhala' (Sikh Rehat Maryada)
5.point: The Sikh standing prayer, the Ardas, ends by asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all: everyone, not just Sikhs, even the people you're against.
5.script: A battle near Anandpur. In the dust, one Sikh, Bhai Ghanaiya, walks the field with a water bag. He kneels by a wounded Sikh, and gives him water. Then he kneels by a wounded enemy soldier. And gives him water too. Some Sikhs were furious. They took him to the Guru: he's helping the other side! Ghanaiya answered, as the story is told: I didn't see sides. I saw the same light in every face. And the Guru didn't punish him. He gave him a balm, to tend their wounds too. That's the heart of the Sikh standing prayer, the Ardas. It ends with three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not just us. Even the person you're not speaking to.
5.drop: Then he kneels by a wounded enemy soldier.
beats: He kneels by a wounded Sikh
Then he kneels by a wounded enemy soldier.
And the Guru didn't punish him.
pictures: Picture 1: Dusk after a battle near Anandpur. A dusty field, smoke drifting, broken spears, soldiers lying or sitting exhausted (no blood, no wounds visible). Bhai Ghanaiya walks among them, white clothes, goatskin water bag on his shoulder. Wide, orange-grey light.
Picture 2: Ghanaiya kneels and lifts the head of a tired Sikh soldier in saffron and blue, pouring water from the bag to his lips. Close, gentle, clean faces, no injuries shown.
Picture 3: Ghanaiya kneels beside a Mughal soldier in green and steel, the enemy, who flinches, then drinks from the same bag. Ghanaiya's face is calm and kind. Close, golden rim light.

Picture 4: Evening camp. Angry Sikh soldiers march Ghanaiya by the arms toward a glowing tent entrance, pointing back at the field. Seen from behind the group; the tent's doorway is only warm light, nobody visible inside. No Guru figure.

Picture 5: Close on Ghanaiya's own weathered hands, now holding a small clay pot of balm along with his water bag, lamplight glowing on it, his face softly relieved above. Only his hands; no other hands or figures.

Picture 6: TODAY. A modern gurdwara hall, the sangat standing for the Ardas, palms together. In the middle, Simran, 17, stands beside Biji; Simran's eyes flick to a friend across the room she's clearly been fighting with, and soften. Jas beside her with his navy patka. Warm light, real and quiet.
motion: Slow tracking shot following Ghanaiya through drifting smoke.
Gentle push in as the water pours and the soldier's eyes open.
Slow arc around the two men as the enemy soldier drinks.
Handheld follow from behind as the group strides toward the glowing doorway.
Slow push in on the clay pot as the lamplight flickers.
Slow drift across the standing sangat, settling on Simran as her expression softens.

6.story: Guru Nanak disappears into the river Bein at Sultanpur and returns saying 'there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman', Janamsakhi traditions
6.point: Sikhi is its own religion, begun by Guru Nanak, not a branch of Hinduism or Islam; 'Sikh' means a learner.
6.script: In the town of Sultanpur, a young man named Nanak went down to the river Bein at dawn to bathe, like every day. He walked into the water. And he didn't come out. The town searched. Nets dragged the river. People gave him up for lost. On the third day, he walked out of the river, and for a long time said nothing. Then his first words: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Some hear: under the labels, everyone is made by the one. Others hear: nobody lives up to their label. Either way, a new path began. Its followers are called Sikh. It means learner. So, Hindu or Muslim? Neither. A learner, on a path of its own.
6.close: a learner, on a path *of its own.*
pictures: Picture 1: Sultanpur, around 1500, before dawn. A quiet riverside town of mud-brick houses and a small mosque and temple roofline, mist on the river Bein, a single brass water pot and a folded cloth left on the stone steps. No person on the steps. Blue-grey hush.
Picture 2: The empty river at sunrise: rings spreading on smooth water where someone has just gone under, reeds bending, mist glowing pink. Nobody visible.

Picture 3: Daytime. Townspeople, Hindu and Muslim neighbours side by side, drag a long net through the river from boats and the bank, others calling out and peering into the reeds. Worried faces. Wide and busy.

Picture 4: The third morning. Golden light breaking over the river; a line of fresh wet footprints leads up the stone steps out of the water into the light, and the townspeople on the bank turn toward something just out of frame, astonished. No figure, no silhouette, only footprints and light.

Picture 5: Two groups of neighbours in the town square, one in Hindu dress with tilak, one in Muslim caps, both looking up at each other and then down at themselves, thoughtful, the river light behind them. Mid shot, warm.

Picture 6: TODAY. A school hallway by the lockers. Simran, 17, in an oversized hoodie and chunni, kara on her wrist, explains something to a curious classmate, both laughing; Jas walks past in his navy patka with his skateboard. Bright, real, everyday.
motion: Very slow push in on the water pot as mist drifts across the river.
Locked-off: the rings spread and fade on the water as the reeds sway.
Pan along the bank as the net is hauled and people shout.
Slow tilt up the wet footprints into the rising light.
Gentle push in between the two groups as they look at one another.
Tracking shot past the lockers settling on Simran's laugh.

7.story: Guru Hargobind takes up two swords, miri and piri, at his installation in Amritsar, 1606 (Sikh tradition); the parts of the Khanda emblem
7.point: The Khanda, the Sikh symbol, is a double-edged sword for truth, a circle without end, and two curved swords for the outer and inner life held together.
7.script: Amritsar, 1606. The fifth Guru had just been put to death by the Mughal authorities. His son, only eleven, became the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind. At the ceremony, he was offered the old signs of the role. He asked for something else. Two swords. One for miri, the world: standing up for people, justice, the hard outer life. One for piri, the spirit: prayer, kindness, the inner life. Both, worn together. Look at the Sikh symbol, the Khanda. Those two curved swords wrap around the outside. In the middle, a circle with no beginning and no end, and a double-edged sword that cuts truth from lies. No crown. No face. You've got an inner life and an outer one. Hold them together.
pictures: Picture 1: Amritsar, 1606, grey dawn. The Harmandir Sahib on its pool, early simple form, reflected in still water; a mourning sangat of ordinary Sikhs sits along the walkway, heads bowed, white cloth, quiet grief. No Guru figure.

Picture 2: The ceremony seen from among the crowd: very old Baba Buddha, long white beard, holds out a simple folded cap of wool thread on a cloth, turned toward a space out of frame; the crowd waits. Soft light, the front of the scene out of frame. No Guru, no boy, no figure where the Guru would be.
Picture 3: Close on two swords laid side by side on saffron cloth, one slightly longer, steel catching the morning light, Baba Buddha's old hands lifting them. Only Baba Buddha's hands visible.

Picture 4: Split by a soft light seam: on the left, Sikhs in a town building, defending a gate, helping an old man carry grain (the outer life); on the right, a woman meditating alone by the shining pool at dusk (the inner life). Balanced, warm.

Picture 5: The Khanda emblem in polished steel on a saffron Nishan Sahib flag, high on a tall pole against a blazing blue sky; the two curved swords, the circle and the straight double-edged sword clear. No letters or text anywhere.

Picture 6: TODAY. Outside a suburban gurdwara under the tall flag. Simran, 17, in a denim jacket, fixes a small steel Khanda pendant on Jas's chain before his basketball game; Dad in a navy dastar holds the car keys, Mom and Biji laughing in the background. Golden late-afternoon light, cool and real.
motion: Very slow push across the still water toward the bowed sangat.
Slow push in on Baba Buddha's face and the folded cap as the crowd leans in.
Close slow pan along the two blades as light glints across the steel.
Slow slide from the busy left half to the still right half.
Low-angle hold as the flag ripples and the steel emblem catches the sun.
Gentle push in as the pendant drops into place and Jas grins.

sources_check: Day 1: Guru Granth Sahib, Swayyas of the Bhatts, Ang 1389-1409 (Waheguru repeated in Bhatt Gayand's swayyas, Ang 1402-1404); Japji Sahib, Ang 1-8 (God beyond counting and description)
Day 2: Sikh tradition of Guru Amar Das at Goindwal and the rule 'pehle pangat, phir sangat'; tradition of Emperor Akbar eating in the langar; langar origin at Kartarpur under Guru Nanak
Day 3: Sikh Rehat Maryada (kesh, turban); Sikh tradition on Guru Gobind Singh giving all Sikhs the marks of nobility (turban) as Khalsa identity

Day 4: Sikh tradition of Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur; names and origins of the Panj Pyare (Daya Singh of Lahore, Dharam Singh near Delhi, Himmat Singh of Puri, Mohkam Singh of Dwarka, Sahib Singh of Bidar); Sikh Rehat Maryada
Day 5: Sikh tradition of Bhai Ghanaiya at Anandpur (water and marham/balm); Ardas as in the Sikh Rehat Maryada ('Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala')
Day 6: Janamsakhi traditions (Puratan and Bhai Bala) of the river Bein at Sultanpur and 'na koi Hindu, na koi Musalman'; Encyclopaedia of Sikhism on 'Sikh' from Sanskrit shishya

Day 7: Sikh tradition of Guru Hargobind's installation in 1606 and the two swords of miri and piri (Baba Buddha officiating); Encyclopaedia of Sikhism on the Khanda emblem; Sikh Rehat Maryada on the Nishan Sahib
risks: Day 1: 'their poems break into one cry: wahe guru' is a vivid framing. Waheguru appears mainly in Bhatt Gayand's swayyas (to Guru Ram Das); the Bhatts' wider praise uses many words. Scholar should confirm the framing is fair, and that saying the Bhatts 'came to the Sikh Gurus' (they came in Guru Arjan's time and praised the first five) is acceptable.

Day 2: Akbar eating in the langar before meeting Guru Amar Das is Sikh tradition, not documented in Mughal records; the script says the rule but not who stated it. Check 'first the meal, then the meeting' as a fair rendering of 'pehle pangat, phir sangat'.

Day 3: the claim that in the Gurus' time fine turbans marked kings and nobles (and not farmers or barbers) simplifies history: commoners also wore head cloths. 'Asked his Sikhs to keep their hair uncut ... made the turban part of who they are' should be checked for fairness to Sikhs who wear a scarf or do not wear a turban (the script keeps it general).

Day 4: the Guru's spoken question is the traditional wording, quoted as tradition. The script keeps 'the tellings differ' about the tent; confirm Daya Ram as 'shopkeeper' (Khatri) and the order of the other four's professions.

Day 5: Bhai Ghanaiya's reply ('I saw the same light in every face') is a paraphrase of a traditional answer (often 'I saw only the Guru in every face'); the script presents it 'as the story is told'. Note that the Ardas text does not mention Ghanaiya; the script links them by spirit only. Pictures avoid blood and wounds.

Day 6: Guru Nanak's three days in the Bein are Janamsakhi tradition (details like nets dragging the river vary between Janamsakhis). The two readings of 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' are given side by side, as in the lesson, without choosing.

Day 7: 'put to death by the Mughal authorities' for Guru Arjan, his son's age (about eleven), and Baba Buddha offering the seli cap are tradition; confirm wording. The Khanda's two-swords-as-miri-piri reading is the common one; the emblem took its present form much later, so the script says 'those two curved swords' rather than claiming Guru Hargobind designed it.

Picture rule: every Guru is kept fully out of frame (no figure, back, hands, shadow or silhouette). Painters must also avoid putting a figure on the platform (day 4), in the tent doorway (days 4, 5), on the river steps (day 6) or where the boy Guru would stand (day 7). Day 5 picture 5 shows only Ghanaiya's hands holding the balm, never the giver's.
